title: PLCs: How They're Different From a Normal Computer
oneLiner: One control job, one endless, predictable loop, on purpose -- why industrial control isn't scheduled the way a laptop is.
keyTakeaway: A PLC trades a general computer's flexibility for a deterministic guarantee (same inputs, same steps, same timing, every time) -- the exact same instructions run in the exact same order, every single scan, with a bounded worst-case time. That predictability, not raw performance, is what industrial control actually needs.
explanation:
A laptop or server runs an operating system that juggles many programs at once -- a scheduler interrupts whatever's running, swaps in another process, and comes back later, which is why background tasks, more browser tabs, or a busy network can make any single program's timing unpredictable. A PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) does the opposite on purpose: it runs its control program forever, in a loop called the scan cycle -- read every input, execute the entire program top to bottom, write every output, do housekeeping, then start over -- typically tens to hundreds of times per second, with a scan time that's measured and bounded, not just "usually fast." Nothing unrelated gets a turn. Many PLCs do run a small real-time OS underneath, and larger controllers can split the logic into several programs and TASKS (IEC 61131-3 defines cyclic/periodic and event tasks, each with a fixed priority), but every task still runs its programs top to bottom on a fixed schedule, so the timing stays bounded. The examples in this track use a single task, so picture one loop.

The program itself usually isn't written in C# or Python -- it's ladder logic, a visual language that looks like an electrical relay diagram (rungs, contacts, coils) rather than lines of code, because PLCs replaced physical relay panels and the engineers and electricians maintaining them already read schematics, not source code. Inputs and outputs are also handled differently at the hardware level: a PLC has dedicated digital and analog I/O modules wired directly to sensors and actuators (devices that move or switch something: motors, valves, relays) (a proximity switch, a 4-20mA pressure transducer, a motor starter coil), read and written as a batch each scan into an input/output image table -- rather than a general computer's abstracted peripherals accessed through OS drivers whenever a program happens to ask.

The result is a machine built for one job: react to the physical world at a guaranteed, predictable pace, and keep running through heat, vibration, and dust that would kill a normal PC (no fan or spinning drive in most PLCs -- solid-state, sealed, rated for a much wider temperature range). A watchdog timer forces a fault state if a scan ever takes too long, because in industrial control "the program froze for a second" isn't a minor bug -- it can mean a motor kept running past when it should have stopped. Networking on top of this (Modbus, EtherNet/IP, fieldbus protocols) and ladder logic itself are worth their own lessons -- this one is about the execution model underneath both.
